title: Tagalog grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Tagalog, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. The examples are the Tagalog of Manila as people really speak it, polite where it should be, with the odd English word where Filipinos use one.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Tagalog conversation.
lessons.topic: Sentences without “am, is, are”; {{ako}} “I”, {{ikaw}} and {{ka}} “you”; {{si}} before a name

goal.t: Kumusta! Ako si Ana. Taga-Maynila ako.
goal.tr: Hi! I'm Ana. I'm from Manila.

blocks.p: Look at what is missing in this conversation: Tagalog has no word for “am”, “is” or “are”. {{Taga-Maynila ako}} is, word for word, “from-Manila I”. And look at the order: the new information (from Manila) comes **first**, and “I” comes after it.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Manila.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

blocks.p: **I and you.** {{ako}} is “I”. “You” has two forms that mean the same: {{ikaw}} when it stands alone or comes first ({{Ikaw?}} “And you?”), and the short {{ka}} after another word ({{Taga-saan ka?}} “Where are you from?”).

table: alone, or first in the sentence

blocks.p: **Your name.** {{Ako si Ana.}} “I'm Ana.” The little word {{si}} goes before a person's name: {{si Ben}}, {{si Maria}}. It has no English translation: it just says “a name comes next”.
**Where you're from.** {{taga-}} means “from (a place)”: {{taga-Cebu}} “from Cebu”, {{taga-saan?}} “from where?”. It comes first, then the pronoun: {{Taga-Cebu ako.}}

ex.note: a question just by raising your voice at the end

blocks.tip: {{Kumusta}} comes from Spanish “¿cómo está?” and works as both “hello” and “how are you?”. Filipinos also say “Hi!” and “Hello!”, in English, all the time.

mistakes.why: A person's name needs {{si}} before it.
The new information comes first and {{ako}} after it: “from-Manila I”.
After another word, “you” is the short {{ka}}.

practice.why: {{taga-}} “from”, then {{ako}} “I”. ({{Ako si Maynila}} would make Manila your name, and {{ka}} is “you”.)

practice.q: You're Mark, from Quezon City. Choose your replies.

lines.why: About yourself, say {{ako}}: {{Ikaw si Mark}} is “You're Mark”.
{{ako}} is “I”; {{ka}} would be “you”.

practice.q: Ask someone your age: “Where are you from?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{Kumusta! Ako si…}}

answers.t: Kumusta! Ako si John. Taga-Chicago ako.
answers.tr: Hi! I'm John. I'm from Chicago.

answers.t: Hi! Ako si Emma. Taga-London ako.
answers.tr: Hi! I'm Emma. I'm from London.

lessons.title: Speak politely to older people and strangers
lessons.summary: Add {{po}} and say {{opo}} to show respect, as every Filipino does with elders, strangers and customers.

goal.t: Magandang umaga po! Ako po si Ana.
goal.note: said to someone older: {{po}} shows respect

dialog.t: Magandang hapon din. Ikaw si Ana?
dialog.tr: Good afternoon to you too. Are you Ana?

blocks.p: Filipinos show respect with one small word: {{po}}. Say it to anyone older than you, to strangers, to customers and to people in charge. It has no English translation: think of it as the “sir” or “ma'am” that goes into every sentence. Without it you can sound rude to an older person, even when your words are kind.
**Yes.** The polite “yes” is {{opo}}. Plain {{oo}} is for friends, for family your age and for children.
**Where {{po}} goes.** Early in the sentence, right after the first word or phrase: {{Salamat po.}} {{Ako po si Ana.}} {{Taga-Cebu po ako.}} It comes before {{ako}}, never after it at the end.
**A polite “you”.** With {{po}}, “you” usually becomes {{kayo}}, which is also “you” for several people: {{Taga-saan po kayo?}} “Where are you from?”, said to someone older.

ex.note: polite; to a friend: {{Ano ang pangalan mo?}}
for a small trouble: bumping into someone, being late

blocks.tip: Older people, even strangers, are called by family words: {{Lola}} “Grandma”, {{Tita}} “Auntie”, {{Kuya}} “big brother” (a young man: a driver, a guard), {{Ate}} “big sister” (a young woman: a shop assistant). {{Salamat po, Kuya!}} is how you thank a jeepney driver. {{Aling}} and {{Mang}} go before an older woman's and man's first name: {{Aling Rosa}}, {{Mang Jose}}.

mistakes.why: To an older person, “yes” is {{opo}}.
{{po}} comes early: after the first word, before {{ako}}.

practice.q: A grandmother asks if you're hungry. “Yes” is…
practice.why: {{opo}} is the polite yes. ({{po}} on its own isn't “yes”.)

practice.tr: Where are you from? (to someone older)

practice.q: Your friend's father opens the door. Choose your replies.

lines.why: He's older: {{opo}}, and {{po}} in the sentence.
“Thank you” is {{salamat}}; {{po}} makes it polite.

practice.q: Thank a jeepney driver (a young man).
Your turn: greet an older neighbor in the morning and say who you are, politely.

answers.t: Magandang umaga po! Ako po si Sarah.
answers.tr: Good morning! I'm Sarah.

answers.t: Magandang umaga po! Ako po si Tom. Taga-Amerika po ako.
answers.tr: Good morning! I'm Tom. I'm from America.

lessons.title: Say what someone is and what they're like
lessons.summary: Say someone's job, where they're from and what they're like: “My mom is a teacher. She's kind.”
lessons.topic: The describing word first; {{siya}} “he, she”; the markers {{si}} and {{ang}}

goal.t: Guro ang nanay ko. Mabait siya.
goal.tr: My mom is a teacher. She's kind.

dialog.tr: Yes, I'm a teacher. And you?
Oh, Ana is a student too!

blocks.p: Again there's no “is”: {{Guro siya}} is “teacher she”. The word that says **what** someone is (a teacher, kind, Filipino) comes first; **who** comes after it.
**He or she: one word.** {{siya}} means both “he” and “she”. Tagalog doesn't say whether the person is a man or a woman: the conversation does. {{Mabait siya}} is “He's kind” or “She's kind”.
**Naming who.** After the describing word comes who you're talking about: a pronoun ({{ako}}, {{ka}}, {{siya}}), {{si}} and a name, or {{ang}} and a word like “mother” or “teacher”.

blocks.means: a little word that comes before a word or a name and shows its job in the sentence. {{si}} (before names) and {{ang}} (before other words) mark who or what the sentence is about.

blocks.p: {{ang}} is often “the”, and {{ang nanay ko}} is “my mom”. Use {{si}} for a name (and for {{Lola}}, {{Nanay}}, {{Tita}} used as names), {{ang}} for everything else.
**What someone is like.** Many describing words start with {{ma-}}: {{mabait}} “kind”, {{matalino}} “smart”, {{masaya}} “happy”, {{maganda}} “beautiful”, {{masipag}} “hard-working”.

blocks.tip: In writing and speeches you'll see the order turned round, with {{ay}} in the middle: {{Siya ay guro.}} It means the same, but in conversation say {{Guro siya.}}

mistakes.why: What someone is comes first, then who: “teacher she”.
A name (and {{Lola}} used as a name) needs {{si}}.
A word like “mom” needs {{ang}} when it's who the sentence is about.

practice.why: Before a word that isn't a name: {{ang}}.

practice.q: Your friend's grandmother asks about you. Choose your replies.

lines.why: What you are comes first: {{estudyante po ako}}.
{{Salamat po}}: thank you, politely.

practice.q: Your turn: say what you are and what you're like, then the same about a friend. Start with what you are: {{… ako.}}

answers.t: Estudyante ako. Masaya ako.
answers.tr: I'm a student. I'm happy.

answers.t: Nars si Kate. Mabait siya.
answers.tr: Kate is a nurse. She's kind.

answers.t: Doktor ako. Masipag ako.
answers.tr: I'm a doctor. I'm hard-working.

lessons.title: Ask yes-or-no questions and answer them
lessons.summary: Turn any sentence into a question with {{ba}}, and say yes, no and not: “Are you tired?” “No, I'm not tired.”

dialog.t: Oo. Ikaw, estudyante ka rin ba?
dialog.tr: Yes. What about you, are you a student too?

blocks.p: **Asking.** Add {{ba}} and a sentence becomes a yes-or-no question: {{Estudyante ka.}} “You're a student.” → {{Estudyante ka ba?}} “Are you a student?”. In everyday speech you can also leave {{ba}} out and just raise your voice at the end.

{{ba}} goes **early**, right after the first word. When the short {{ka}} is there too, {{ka}} comes first: {{Pagod ka ba?}} “Are you tired?”. Before a longer pronoun like {{siya}}, and before {{si}} or {{ang}}, {{ba}} comes first: {{Pagod ba siya?}} “Is she tired?”, {{Guro ba si Ben?}} “Is Ben a teacher?”.
**Answering.** {{oo}} “yes” ({{opo}} with respect), {{hindi}} “no”. {{hindi}} is also “not”: put it **first**, and a pronoun jumps to right after it: {{Hindi ako pagod.}} “I'm not tired.”
Only the pronouns ({{ako}}, {{ka}}, {{siya}}…) jump forward after {{hindi}}. A name with {{si}}, or a word with {{ang}}, stays at the end: {{Hindi pagod si Ben.}}

blocks.tip: {{Po?}} on its own, with a rising voice, means “Sorry, what did you say?”: the polite way to ask someone to repeat.

mistakes.why: {{hindi}} comes first, and {{ako}} right after it.
The short {{ka}} comes before {{ba}}.
After {{hindi}}, the pronoun jumps up: {{hindi ako}}.

practice.why: {{hindi}} first, then the pronoun, then the describing word.

practice.q: Your neighbor's grandmother asks you questions. Choose your replies.

lines.why: “No” is {{hindi}}, with {{po}} for Lola.
{{opo}} to an elder, and what you are comes first.

practice.q: Your turn: ask a new friend two yes-or-no questions, then answer one about yourself with {{hindi}}.

answers.t: Estudyante ka ba? Taga-Maynila ka ba? Hindi ako taga-Maynila.
answers.tr: Are you a student? Are you from Manila? I'm not from Manila.

answers.t: Pilipino ka ba? Guro ka ba? Hindi ako guro.
answers.tr: Are you Filipino? Are you a teacher? I'm not a teacher.

lessons.title: Point at things and name them
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?”, name what you see near and far, and talk about more than one.

goal.t: Ano ito? Ano ang tawag dito sa Tagalog?
goal.tr: What's this? What's it called in Tagalog?

blocks.p: Tagalog has **three** words for “this” and “that”, by distance: {{ito}} near me, {{iyan}} near you, {{iyon}} far from both of us. So when the vendor holds the fruit, you say {{iyan}} and she says {{ito}}.

**Naming.** As always, the new information comes first: {{Mangga ito.}} “This is a mango.” In a question, {{ano}} “what” takes the place of the answer: {{Ano ito?}} “What's this?” → {{Saging ito.}} “This is a banana.”

blocks.means: a word for a person, an animal, a thing or a place: mango, teacher, house, Manila.

blocks.p: **The.** Before a noun, {{ang}} is often “the”: {{Masarap ang mangga.}} “The mango is delicious.” Tagalog has no word for “a”: {{mangga}} alone is “a mango”.
**More than one.** Put {{mga}} before the noun: {{ang mga libro}} “the books”. It's said “ma-NGA”. {{ito}}, {{iyan}} and {{iyon}} don't change: {{Mga libro ito.}} “These are books.”

ex.t: Ano ang tawag dito sa Tagalog?

blocks.tip: In speech the three are often cut short: {{'to}}, {{'yan}}, {{'yon}}. {{Ano 'yan?}} is how most people actually say “What's that?”.

mistakes.why: What it is comes first: “mango this”.

mistakes.tr: What's this? (the thing in your own hand)
mistakes.why: Near you, the speaker, it's {{ito}}. {{iyan}} is for something near the person you're talking to.
The noun the sentence is about needs {{ang}}.

practice.q: The bag is in your friend's hands. You ask…
practice.why: Near the person you're talking to: {{iyan}}.
Before a noun that isn't a name: {{ang}}.
{{mga}} before a noun: more than one.

practice.q: At the market: choose your replies.

lines.why: To ask what's near her: {{Ano po iyan?}}
{{ba}} comes after the first word.

practice.q: Point at a church far away and say: “That's a church.”
Your turn: name three things: one near you, one near a friend, one far away.

answers.t: Libro ito. Bag iyan. Bahay iyon.
answers.tr: This is a book. That's a bag. That's a house over there.

answers.t: Kape ito. Tubig iyan. Jeep iyon.
answers.tr: This is coffee. That's water. That's a jeepney over there.

lessons.title: Talk about yourselves and other people
lessons.summary: Say “we”, “you all” and “they”, and choose the right “we”: Tagalog has two.

goal.note: “we” including the person you're talking to

blocks.p: English has one “we”; Tagalog has two, and the difference matters. {{kami}} is “we, **not you**”: me and my group, talking to someone outside it. {{tayo}} is “we, **including you**”: you and me together. Ben tells Liza {{estudyante kami}} (he and his friends), then, once she's a student too, {{pare-pareho tayo}} (all of them, Liza included).

table: {{Mga estudyante ba kayo?}} Are you students?

blocks.p: Ask yourself one question: is the person I'm talking to part of this “we”? Yes: {{tayo}}. No: {{kami}}.
**Several names.** Before two or more names, {{si}} becomes {{sina}}: {{sina Mark at Ana}} “Mark and Ana”. ({{at}} is “and”.)

ex.t: Mga guro sina Mark at Ana.

ex.note: to several people, or politely to one

blocks.tip: Ask a group of Filipinos where they're from and you'll hear {{kami}}; when they invite you to eat with them, you'll hear {{tayo}}. The day someone says {{tayo}} about you, you're one of the group.

mistakes.why: The teacher isn't a student: “we, not you” is {{kami}}.
Before two or more names, {{si}} becomes {{sina}}.

practice.q: You tell a waiter about you and your friends: “We're hungry.”
You and your friend are both tired. You say to your friend: “We're tired!”

practice.tr: Where are you from? (to someone older)

practice.q: Two tourists talk to you and your sister. Choose your replies.

lines.why: The tourists aren't Filipino: {{kami}}, “we, not you”.
“You (all)” is {{kayo}}.

practice.q: Your turn: say where you and your family are from, then tell a new Filipino friend “We're friends!”

answers.t: Taga-Texas kami. Magkaibigan tayo!
answers.tr: We're from Texas. We're friends!

answers.t: Taga-Sydney kami. Estudyante kami. Magkaibigan tayo!
answers.tr: We're from Sydney. We're students. We're friends!

lessons.title: Say what you want
lessons.summary: Ask for things and say what you want to do: “I'd like coffee.” “I want to eat adobo.”
lessons.topic: {{gusto}} and {{ayaw}} with {{ko}}, {{mo}}, {{niya}}; {{ng}} “some, a”; {{gusto kong}} + a verb (the linker {{-ng}})

dialog.t: Gutom ka ba? Ano ang gusto mo?
dialog.tr: Are you hungry? What do you want?

dialog.t: Ayoko ng adobo. Gusto kong kumain ng sinigang.
dialog.tr: I don't want adobo. I want to eat sinigang.

blocks.p: **Wanting a thing.** {{gusto}} “want” comes first, then who wants, then what: {{Gusto ko ng kape.}} “I want coffee.” Word for word: “want I some-coffee”. Look at the “I”: not {{ako}}, but {{ko}}.

**A second set of pronouns.** After {{gusto}}, “I” is {{ko}}, “you” is {{mo}}, “he/she” is {{niya}}. This set has other jobs too (“my”, “your”: lesson 10); for now, use it after {{gusto}} and {{ayaw}}.

table: {{Gusto ko ng tubig.}} I want water.
{{Ano ang gusto mo?}} What do you want?
{{Gusto niya ng kape.}} She wants coffee.
{{Gusto namin ng pizza.}} We want pizza.
{{Ano ang gusto natin?}} What do we want?
{{Ano po ang gusto ninyo?}} What would you like?
{{Gusto nila ng kanin.}} They want rice.

blocks.p: **{{ng}}: some, a.** The thing you want takes the marker {{ng}}, said “nang”: {{ng kape}} “(some) coffee”, {{ng adobo}}. {{ng}} marks a thing that isn't what the sentence is about.
**Not wanting.** {{ayaw}} is “not want, not like”: {{Ayaw ko ng kape.}} In speech {{ayaw ko}} becomes one word, {{ayoko}}: {{Ayoko!}} “I don't want to!”

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: eat, go, sleep, want.
a little joining piece, {{-ng}} or {{na}}, that ties two words together. Tagalog needs it in many places where English just puts words side by side.

blocks.p: **Wanting to do something.** Put the verb after {{gusto ko}}, tied on with the linker {{-ng}}: {{gusto ko}} + {{kumain}} → {{gusto kong kumain}} “I want to eat”. {{ko}}, {{mo}} and {{niya}} end in a vowel, so the linker is just {{-ng}} added on: {{gusto mong}}, {{gusto niyang}}. Even {{ba}} takes it: {{Gusto mo bang kumain?}}
Some verbs to start with, in the form that goes after {{gusto}}: {{kumain}} eat, {{uminom}} drink, {{matulog}} sleep, {{umuwi}} go home, {{pumunta}} go, {{mag-aral}} study.

ex.tr: Do you want something to drink?
He doesn't want to go home.
We want to go to Boracay.
ex.note: {{namin}} ends in n: the n becomes {{-ng}}

blocks.tip: {{gusto}} is also “like”: {{Gusto ko ang Maynila.}} “I like Manila.” With {{ang}} it's something particular you like; with {{ng}}, some of something you want. In a shop, {{Gusto ko ng…}} is fine; even more polite is {{Pabili po ng…}} (lesson 20).

mistakes.why: After {{gusto}}, “I” is {{ko}}, not {{ako}}.
{{ko}} and the verb are tied with the linker: {{kong}}.

practice.why: Before a verb, {{ko}} takes the linker: {{kong}}.

practice.tr: Do you want something to drink?

practice.q: At a carinderia (a small eatery). Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{gusto ko}}, with {{po}} to be polite.

options: Opo, gusto ko rin po ng kanin.
lines.why: {{gusto ko… ng kanin}}; {{rin}} is “too”.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you want and one you don't. Use {{Gusto ko ng…}}, {{Gusto kong…}} and {{Ayoko ng…}}

answers.t: Gusto ko ng kape. Gusto kong matulog. Ayoko ng ampalaya.
answers.tr: I'd like coffee. I want to sleep. I don't like bitter gourd.

answers.t: Gusto kong mag-aral ng Tagalog. Gusto ko ng mangga. Ayoko ng balut.
answers.tr: I want to study Tagalog. I'd like a mango. I don't want balut.

lessons.title: Say what you have and what there is
lessons.summary: Say what you have, ask if there's something, and answer “there isn't”: “Do you have any brothers or sisters?” “I have two.”

dialog.tr: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

dialog.t: Oo, mayroon akong dalawang kapatid. Ikaw?
dialog.tr: Yes, I have two. And you?

dialog.t: Wala akong kapatid. Pero may tatlong aso ako!
dialog.tr: I don't have any. But I have three dogs!

blocks.p: One word does two jobs: {{may}} is both “there is” and “have”. {{May aso.}} “There's a dog.” {{May aso ako.}} “I have a dog.” (Word for word: “there-is dog I”.)

**Three words.** {{may}} goes straight before the thing: {{may aso}}. {{mayroon}} (in speech {{meron}}) means the same, but the pronoun comes right after it, tied on with the linker: {{mayroon akong aso}}. {{mayroon}} is also the answer on its own: {{Mayroon.}} “Yes, there is / Yes, I do.” {{wala}} is the opposite, “there isn't, don't have”, and works like {{mayroon}}: {{wala akong aso}}.
Look at {{walang aso}}: when the thing comes straight after {{wala}}, the linker ties them together. To ask, add {{ba}}: {{May tubig ba?}} “Is there any water?” The answers: {{Mayroon.}} or {{Wala.}}

**Numbers.** {{isa}} 1, {{dalawa}} 2, {{tatlo}} 3, {{apat}} 4, {{lima}} 5, {{anim}} 6, {{pito}} 7, {{walo}} 8, {{siyam}} 9, {{sampu}} 10. Before a noun they take the linker: {{dalawang aso}} “two dogs”, {{isang kotse}} “one car, a car”. After a consonant, the linker is a separate {{na}}: {{apat na aso}}, {{anim na anak}}. With a number, {{mga}} isn't needed.

ex.t: May apat na kuwarto ang bahay.
ex.note: the owner can be {{ang}} + a noun, at the end

blocks.tip: {{wala}} is one of the most useful words in Tagalog: {{Wala na.}} “There's none left.” {{Wala pa.}} “None yet.” {{Wala lang.}} “Nothing, never mind.”

mistakes.why: After {{mayroon}} and {{wala}}, the pronoun is tied to the thing with the linker: {{akong}}.
Straight after {{wala}}, add the linker: {{walang}}.
A number is tied to its noun with the linker: {{dalawang}}.

practice.why: After a vowel, the linker is {{-ng}} added on: {{tatlong}}.
After a consonant, the linker is a separate {{na}}.

practice.q: At a sari-sari store (a small corner shop). Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{may}} straight before the thing, {{ba}} for the question, {{po}} to be polite.
{{Wala na}}: there's none left. Just thank her.

practice.q: Your turn: say what family or pets you have, and one thing you don't have.

answers.t: Mayroon akong isang kapatid at dalawang pusa. Wala akong kotse.
answers.tr: I have one sibling and two cats. I don't have a car.

answers.t: May tatlong anak ako. Wala akong aso.
answers.tr: I have three kids. I don't have a dog.

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Put describing words with nouns (“a big house”, “a kind person”) and react: “How beautiful!”
lessons.topic: The linker {{na}} / {{-ng}} between an adjective and its noun; {{Ang ganda!}}; {{napaka-}}, {{sobrang}}

goal.t: Ang ganda ng bagong bag mo!
goal.tr: Your new bag is so nice!

dialog.t: Ang ganda ng bagong bag mo!
dialog.tr: Your new bag is so nice!
No! It's just a simple bag.

blocks.p: **A describing word on its own** comes first, as you know: {{Malaki ang bahay.}} “The house is big.” But to put it **with** a noun, “a big house”, Tagalog ties the two together with the linker: {{malaking bahay}}.

blocks.means: a describing word: big, kind, new, delicious.

blocks.p: The linker is {{-ng}} added on after a vowel ({{malaki}} → {{malaking bahay}}), and after an n, which it replaces ({{mayaman}} “rich” → {{mayamang tao}} “a rich person”). After any other consonant it's a separate {{na}}: {{mabait na tao}} “a kind person”.

**Either order.** The adjective can come before or after the noun, always with the linker in between: {{malaking bahay}} or {{bahay na malaki}}, both “a big house”. The first is more common in speech.

**Wow!** To react, put {{ang}} before the adjective without its {{ma-}}: {{Ang ganda!}} “How beautiful!” ({{maganda}}), {{Ang init!}} “It's so hot!” ({{mainit}}), {{Ang sarap!}} “So good!” ({{masarap}}). Add {{ng}} and what you mean: {{Ang sarap ng adobo!}} “The adobo is so good!”
**Very.** {{napaka-}} + the adjective without {{ma-}}: {{napakaganda}} “very beautiful”. In everyday speech, also {{sobrang}}: {{sobrang init}} “really hot”.

ex.t: Gusto ko ng malamig na tubig.

blocks.tip: {{Ang}} + a describing word is everywhere in Filipino conversation, and the easiest way to sound natural: {{Ang galing!}} “Great job!”, {{Ang cute!}} “So cute!”, {{Ang mahal!}} “So expensive!”.

mistakes.why: An adjective and its noun need the linker: {{malaki}} + {{-ng}}.
After a consonant (here t), the linker is a separate {{na}}.
In a “wow” sentence, {{ang}} goes with the word without {{ma-}}. ({{ang maganda}} is “the beautiful one”.)

practice.why: {{malamig}} ends in a consonant: a separate {{na}}.

practice.q: How do you say “a new car”?
practice.why: {{bago}} ends in a vowel: {{-ng}} added on.

practice.q: The food is delicious. You say…
Your friend's grandmother cooked lunch. Choose your replies.

options: Salamat po. Ang sarap po ng adobo ninyo!
lines.why: {{Ang sarap ng…}}, with {{po}} for Lola.
{{napaka-}}: very delicious. ({{napakasarap ka}} would be “you're very delicious”!)

practice.q: Your turn: describe your home or your city with two adjectives, then react to something you like with {{Ang…!}}

answers.t: Maliit na bahay ito, pero maganda. Ang ganda ng hardin!
answers.tr: It's a small house, but it's nice. The garden is so pretty!

answers.t: Malaking lungsod ang Maynila. Ang init dito!
answers.tr: Manila is a big city. It's so hot here!

lessons.title: Say whose something is
lessons.summary: Say “my”, “your”, “Ana's” and “mine”: “Is this your phone?” “No, it's Ana's.”
lessons.topic: {{ko}}, {{mo}}, {{niya}} after the noun; {{aking}}, {{iyong}} before it; {{akin}} “mine”; {{ng}} and {{ni}} for the owner; {{kanino}}

goal.t: Ito ang bahay ng lola ko.

blocks.p: **My, your, his.** The pronouns you know from {{gusto}} ({{ko}}, {{mo}}, {{niya}}…) also mean “my, your, his/her”. They go **after** the noun: {{bahay ko}} “my house”, {{pangalan mo}} “your name”, {{anak niya}} “his/her child”.
The middle column, tied on with the linker, means the same as the first. It's more common in writing and in songs ({{aking mahal}} “my love”); in conversation, put {{ko}}, {{mo}}… after the noun.
**Mine, yours.** The third set stands alone: {{Akin ito.}} “This is mine.” {{Iyo ba iyan?}} “Is that yours?”

**Someone's.** With a name, the owner takes {{ni}}: {{bahay ni Ana}} “Ana's house”. With any other noun, {{ng}}: {{bahay ng lola ko}} “my grandma's house”, word for word “house of grandma my”. And “Ana's” on its own is {{kay Ana}}: {{Kay Ana ito.}} “This is Ana's.” To ask, {{Kanino ito?}} “Whose is this?”
“This umbrella” is {{ang payong na ito}}: {{ito}} is tied to the noun with the linker, like an adjective.

ex.t: Ito ang bahay ng lola ko.

blocks.tip: Now you've met the three families of markers: {{ang}} / {{si}} (who or what the sentence is about), {{ng}} / {{ni}} (of, some, an owner) and {{sa}} / {{kay}} (to, at, for; next lesson). Most Tagalog sentences are built from these.

mistakes.why: {{ko}} goes after the noun.
With a name, the owner takes {{ni}}, not {{ng}}.
On its own, “mine” is {{akin}}.

practice.why: An owner that isn't a name: {{ng}}.

practice.q: Someone asks {{Kanino ito?}} about your phone. You say…
practice.why: “Mine” on its own is {{akin}}. ({{Ako iyan}} is “That's me”!)

practice.q: At a party, your friend finds a bag. Choose your replies.

options: Hindi akin iyan. Kay Ana yata.
Hindi ako iyan. Si Ana yata.
lines.why: “Not mine” is {{hindi akin}}; “Ana's” is {{kay Ana}}.
{{Walang anuman}} is “You're welcome”: word for word “there's nothing”.

practice.q: Your turn: name two things you own, and one that belongs to someone in your family.

answers.t: Cellphone ko ito. Akin ang bag na ito. Kotse ng tatay ko iyon.
answers.tr: This is my phone. This bag is mine. That's my dad's car.

answers.t: Libro ko ito. Bahay ng lola ko iyon.
answers.tr: This is my book. That's my grandma's house.

lessons.title: Say where people and things are
lessons.summary: Ask where something is and say where: “Where's the bathroom?” “Upstairs, next to Ben's room.”
lessons.topic: {{nasa}} and {{nasaan}}; {{nandito}}, {{nandiyan}}, {{nandoon}}; {{sa}}, {{kay}} and place words ({{sa loob ng}}, {{sa tabi ng}}…)

dialog.t: Nasa itaas, sa tabi ng kuwarto ni Ben.
Salamat po. E si Ben po, nasaan siya?
dialog.tr: Thank you. And Ben, where is he?

blocks.p: **Where something is**: {{nasa}} + the place. {{Nasa kusina si Nanay.}} “Mom is in the kitchen.” As always, the new information (where) comes first. {{nasa}} is “in”, “at” and “on” all at once.
**Asking**: {{nasaan}} “where is?”. {{Nasaan ang susi?}} “Where's the key?” Answer with {{nasa}}: {{Nasa mesa.}} “On the table.”
**Here and there** go with {{ito}}, {{iyan}} and {{iyon}}: {{nandito}} “(it's) here”, {{nandiyan}} “(it's) there, near you”, {{nandoon}} “(it's) over there”. {{Nandito ako!}} “I'm here!”

**{{sa}}**, the third marker, is for places and directions, and for the people you do something to or for: {{sa Maynila}} “in Manila, to Manila”, {{sa bahay}} “at home”. With a name it's {{kay}}: {{kay Ana}} “to Ana, at Ana's”.
**Exact places**: {{sa}} + a place word + {{ng}} + the thing. {{sa ilalim ng mesa}} “under the table”, word for word “at the underneath of the table”.

ex.t: Nasa ilalim ng mesa ang pusa.
ex.tr: The cat is under the table.

ex.note: what you call out when you arrive; {{na}} is “now, already”

ex.t: Nasa harap ng simbahan ang tindahan.
ex.tr: The store is in front of the church.

blocks.tip: Filipinos call the toilet the {{CR}} (“comfort room”): {{Nasaan po ang CR?}} is the question you'll use most in Manila. In quick speech you'll also hear {{Saan ang CR?}}

mistakes.tr: The key is on the table.
mistakes.why: Where comes first ({{nasa mesa}}), then what.
A place word is tied to the thing with {{ng}}: {{ilalim ng mesa}}.

practice.tr: The cat is under the table.
practice.why: {{ilalim ng mesa}}: “the underneath of the table”.

practice.q: Your friend calls: “Where are you?” You're outside their door. You say…
You can't find your phone. Choose your replies.

lines.why: To ask where: {{nasaan}}.

lines.t: Nandiyan, sa ilalim ng bag mo!

lines.why: {{Oo nga!}} is “Oh, right!”. Ana says {{nandiyan}} because it's near you.

practice.q: Your turn: say where three people or things in your home are right now.

answers.t: Nasa kusina si Nanay. Nasa mesa ang susi. Nasa ilalim ng kama ang pusa.
answers.tr: Mom is in the kitchen. The key is on the table. The cat is under the bed.

answers.t: Nasa trabaho ang asawa ko. Nasa sala ang mga bata. Nandito ako sa kuwarto.
answers.tr: My husband is at work. The kids are in the living room. I'm here in the bedroom.
